narrative:
The model predicted a 72.7% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Placing in the second decile, noticeably below the average of accepted students (around the sixth decile), signaled that your performance lagged behind most successful applicants. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; you finished in the third decile while accepted students averaged the sixth decile. These two early indicators of how you performed relative to your classmates outweighed everything else.

Your undergraduate GPA was the only major factor working in your favor. At 3.50 it sits above the 3.23 average of accepted students, which helped reduce the predicted risk somewhat. However, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the impact of your law-school rankings.

Your LSAT score of 36, family income in the upper-middle bracket, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time played only minor roles and did not meaningfully change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or consider programs that allow you to demonstrate consistent high performance. Raising your class standing in future work will directly address the factors that most hurt your prediction.
